idiom_name: interface type with implicit satisfaction (io.Reader style)
implementation_notes: A Go interface declares a method set and nothing else - it cannot hold data, so the contract is stateless by construction - and any type whose method set includes those methods satisfies it, with no implements clause and no coupling at the declaration site. That is why the contract is usually introduced by the consumer and kept to one or two methods: io.Reader exists because Read([]byte) (int, error) is all a caller needs, and the interface could be named long after the implementations were written. The classic structure is replaced outright - no base class, no constructor, no state: the implementation is a struct (often unexported) holding the state, and a constructor function returns the interface.
pitfalls: Method sets differ by receiver form: T's method set holds only value-receiver methods while *T's adds the pointer-receiver ones, so returning fileReader{} instead of &fileReader{} can silently fail to satisfy an interface.
A typed nil stored in an interface is not a nil interface: err != nil is true for a nil *myError, so constructors must return an untyped nil.

Wide interfaces are hard to implement and hard to fake; Go convention favours one or two methods (the bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction) and returning concrete types from constructors (accept interfaces, return structs).
Satisfaction is implicit, so a mistyped method signature does not fail at the implementation - it fails only where the value is assigned to the interface, and only if such an assignment exists.

variants.name: Interface as a type-set constraint (generics)
variants.idiom_name: type-parameter constraint with type sets (~T, unions)
variants.implementation_notes: Since Go 1.18 an interface may embed arbitrary types, unions and ~T approximations, which makes it a set of types rather than a method set; such an interface may only be used as a type constraint, and the contract is then resolved at compile time with no interface value, no allocation and no dynamic dispatch. This is the type-class-style realization, and it is the only way to state contracts that methods cannot express, such as ordering or arithmetic on a family of types; the Go authors' guidance is to write functions first and add type parameters only where the implementation is identical for every type. Keep the plain method-set interface for open-ended implementations and for anything that has to be stored in one collection.
pitfalls: A generalized interface (unions or ~T) cannot be used as a value type at all, and a type parameter is not an interface value, so generic code cannot fall back to dynamic dispatch.
Methods may be called on a type parameter only when the constraint declares them, even if every type in the set has the method, which forces constraints to be widened for ordinary code.
Type inference usually hides the instantiation; when it fails, the diagnostic names a structural type the caller never wrote.
